extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history and media studies; general readers interested in the development of American newspapers (1860–1892)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts historical standards and evaluative criteria used to judge American newspapers and journalism in the period c.1860–1892, including professionalism, independence, reporting practices, ethics, style, and commercial metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional idea: public service and craft proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: “The professional phases of journalism, as distinguished from its commercial and mechanical elements, may be said to be: first, those which emphasize public service; and, second, those which relate to proficiency in writing and editing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional journalism is defined by service to the public and by skill (writing/editing). Historical exemplars (Franklin, Bryant) illustrate the professional ideal; when newspapers were mere adjuncts of printing establishments professionalism was limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational attainment of journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and writers were increasingly expected to have higher preliminary education: e.g., “the preliminary education of the mass of journalists is much better now... there is scarcely a writer who is not a college graduate; while, indeed, two thirds or more of its reporters are, to use the vague phrase, men of liberal education.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher education and liberal education among staff were cited as markers of professionalism and earned journalism greater respect. Recruitment of college graduates is presented as evidence of professionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from party bonds (independent journalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence from party control: e.g., Greeley’s declaration, White-law Reid’s formulation of 'Independent journalism' and Reid’s list of what independence should end — “concealments... one-sided expositions... assaults... slanders... hesitation to print the news... doctoring the reports of public opinion... half truths.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence means freedom from party discipline so papers can criticize leaders and policies from within; it does not necessarily imply neutrality or always bolting the party. Examples: the 'mugwumps' and Republican papers that refused to support Grant or Blaine in specific elections. Anti-patterns include doctoring reports, slander, withholding news to protect party interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and human-interest orientation of news coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: A shift in emphasis 'from editorial comment and preoccupation with affairs of government to wider fields of news and to more intimate human interests' is presented as characteristic of the era and as a factor weakening partisan control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers that expanded beyond partisan editorializing into broader news and human-interest reporting were seen as more modern and popular; this shift placed more power in reporters' hands and away from politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to public opinion (speed and accuracy of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Samuel Bowles' test: 'the capacity to see quickly and to express correctly the tendencies of public opinion' is cited as 'the test of a true journalist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should quickly perceive public trends and articulate them accurately; this responsiveness is valued as a core professional function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of coloring/shaping the news for partisan ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The text criticizes 'coloring and shaping the news to support partisan attitudes' and notes that this malpractice 'was very widely practised in the seventies and eighties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shaping news to favor a party is condemned; contemporary critics are cited (Nation, North American Review). Ethical reporting should resist partisan distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crusades and civic activism as journalistic practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers engaged in crusades to correct local abuses and promote social welfare—e.g., Tribune's fresh-air fund, World’s pedestal-for-Statue-of-Liberty campaign, free-ice and free-medical-service funds, attacks on monopolies, community improvement programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crusades are presented as an aspect of the New Journalism: public-spirited campaigns and reform efforts that replace some partisan activities. They are examples of newspapers performing public-service functions; both positive (reform) and advocacy dimensions are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensational techniques and 'stunts' (New Journalism methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The era saw the rise of 'New Journalism' characterized by sensational techniques, multiple crusades, price competition, and spectacular 'stunts' (e.g., Stanley expedition publicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such techniques increased circulation and influenced competitors; they include aggressive publicity, spectacle, and human-interest emphasis. They are evaluated both as commercially effective and as altering editorial norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and prohibition of fabrication/hoaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by the New York Herald's 'wild animal hoax' where the paper later admitted: 'The entire story given above is a pure fabrication. Not one word of it is true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrications and hoaxes are ethically wrong and can cause public panic; even if later revealed, they are presented as an anti-pattern that undermines trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness and investment in newsgathering resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of thorough news-gathering: employing many reporters and correspondents, extensive cable dispatches, organizing expeditions (Stanley, DeLong), and claiming to 'print all the news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale investment in correspondents, foreign reporting, and special expeditions is described as a marker of a paper's news leadership and comprehensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of writing, editorial craft, and mentorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun is praised as 'the clever, well-written “newspaper-man's newspaper”' and editors like Selah M. Clarke are noted as 'recognized as one of the best teachers of newspaper work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary presentation, well-trained reporters, strong night and managing editors, and on-the-job mentorship are highlighted as contributors to superior journalistic writing and craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial metrics: circulation, price, and advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation figures, price-per-copy changes, and advertising revenue are treated as key measures of a paper's success—examples include circulation numbers for Herald, Sun, World; price cuts to two cents; and raising advertising rates to offset price changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business decisions (price cuts, news-stand networks, ad-rate adjustments) directly affected reach and profitability; dealers' resistance and organized protests are noted as practical constraints. These metrics are presented as pragmatic criteria for a paper's standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial influence and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial influence (the ability to shape opinion) and consistency of editorial course are implied measures of a paper's standing; e.g., the Sun had 'little influence' editorially though its writers were able, and the Sun's course was 'not... consistent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency and sustained editorial positions contribute to influence; inconsistency or erratic editorial positions reduce editorial impact. Ownership, managerial changes, and editorial personalities affect consistency.
